results.title: US-led coalition ends mission in Iraq
results.description: BAGHDAD — A United States-led coalition deployed in Iraq more than a decade ago to fight jihadists concluded its mission on Wednesday, a move celebrated by the country’s leaders, but which some fear would embolden pro-Iran armed factions. Coalition troops were deployed to Iraq and Syria in 2014 to fight the Islamic State (IS) group, which had seized large swathes of territory, committed massacres, and forced thousands of women and children into slavery. The group was defeated in Iraq in 2017 and in Syria in 2019, but coalition forces stayed on to battle the group’s remnants. The US and Iraq agreed in 2024 to wind down the coalition’s mission, and its troops withdrew gradually from bases across the country, restricting their presence to the autonomous northern Kurdistan region. On Wednesday, the US announced the mission’s formal conclusion. “Today, the United States and our Coalition partners formally concluded Operation Inherent Resolve in Iraq, consistent with the September 2024 US-Iraq joint statement and US national interests,” the Pentagon said in a statement. The US Department of Defense, however, added that it would “continue to provide targeted training and intelligence support to our Iraqi partners.” ‘Sovereignty’ The US-led coalition did not defeat IS alone. Kurdish Peshmerga fighters played an important role in crushing IS, as did powerful Iraqi factions, including pro-Iran groups that have yet to disarm. The Iraqi government, which celebrated the withdrawal, believes it would deprive Iran-backed factions of the excuse they have used to retain their arsenal. But many Iraqis fear the pullout might embolden the pro-Iran factions further and draw the country deeper into the Middle East war. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi hailed the end of the mission as the start of a new chapter. “A new phase has begun, defined by Iraq’s sovereignty, the strength of its institutions, the readiness of its forces, unity of decision-making, and balanced partnerships with its friends,” Zaidi said at a ceremony on Wednesday. He had also declared that Oct. 1 would be celebrated as Sovereignty Day. It is “a national occasion that affirms the completion of Iraq’s path toward sovereignty and consolidates the presence of the state and its institutions,” the heads of Iraq’s executive, legislative and judicial branches said on Monday. They added that “the presence of weapons outside state authority must be addressed ... in line with timelines set by the government, in a manner that strengthens state sovereignty.” Intensified attacks Zaidi, who came to power this year with the US’ blessing, has vowed to reinforce the state’s monopoly on arms and ensure that armed factions hand over their weapons to the state. His government initially set Sept. 30 as the deadline for factions to disarm, but later withdrew the time limit as talks continued to “regulate” weapons — an issue that has fueled division and is expected to take much longer to resolve. With several powerful groups refusing to disarm, senior politicians have intervened and are now hoping to work out a compromise deal. Factions have put forward conditions that include not only the withdrawal of foreign troops, but also an end to American political and economic interference. The powerful Kataeb Hezbollah group said the withdrawal of “the occupation forces ... is a start towards achieving full sovereignty.” But the group also threatened Zaidi’s government. “A government that doesn’t work for the good of its people will be brought down by all possible means,” it said. Pro-Iran groups have long demanded the withdrawal of US troops and have begun targeting them with drones and missiles, triggering US retaliatory strikes that killed several faction commanders over the years. During the Middle East war that began with deadly US-Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, Tehran and allied factions intensified their attacks in Iraq, targeting US-led troops in the Kurdistan region.

results.title: Asean must speak together and work in smaller groups
results.description: SOUTHEAST Asia’s diplomacy with China cannot be left to 11 separate national calculations. Geography and commerce bind the region to China, but power is unequal. Alone, members face Chinese inducements or pressure without regional support. Asean needs multilateral diplomacy to establish what its members will uphold together. Smaller groups can then solve focused problems without weakening that common position. Otherwise, Asean risks being picked off one member at a time, even while its summits continue to proclaim unity. The multilateral foundation is Asean centrality: the discipline of agreeing on principles before engaging China. The Asean-China Plan of Action for 2026–2030 provides a framework spanning security, economic, social, environmental and cultural cooperation. Asean should use it to set priorities, review implementation and benefit communities. The upgraded Asean-China free trade agreement reaches digital and green economies alongside trade. Separate investment offers can tempt governments to mute objections. Members need shared standards on transparency and resilience so economic cooperation strengthens rather than fragments their negotiating position. The South China Sea shows why a common position matters. Persistent disputes make dialogue indispensable, but dialogue cannot mean leaving a state alone when its lawful rights are challenged. Asean should agree in advance how to report incidents, affirm the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea and respond collectively to coercive conduct. It should press China for a substantive, effective Code of Conduct that reduces dangerous encounters, protects lawful rights and provides crisis procedures. A code must not dilute international law or restrict states outside the negotiations. Collective statements need not settle every sovereignty claim. They can establish that pressure against one member concerns the region as a whole, while keeping channels open for de-escalation. Consensus among 11 states can be slow, especially when their exposure to China differs. That difficulty makes preparation more important, not collective diplomacy less necessary. Coastal states with overlapping concerns can coordinate legal analysis, share maritime information, establish coast guard hotlines, and agree on search and rescue, fisheries protection and incident reporting. Such groups should feed their findings into Asean, building a stronger regional position. Where China is ready, they can cooperate on marine science, conservation and safe navigation. The test is whether practical cooperation reinforces Asean’s shared principles when those principles come under pressure. Diplomacy should operate across tracks to make that collective position informed and durable. Track 1 brings officials to formal negotiations. Track 1.5 brings officials together with researchers and practitioners. Track 2 lets scholars, civic groups, business, labor, youth and local governments explore proposals before governments adopt them. Think tanks can test options for a maritime code, environmental safeguards or labor standards. Fisheries communities can describe risks official maps miss. Local administrators can compare flood warnings, disaster response and public health programs. These channels help governments negotiate with knowledge and public legitimacy. Asean Plus Three shows discussion can extend beyond summits. Soft diplomacy also supports regional cohesion. Cultural exchange, education, journalism and youth programs connect neighbors. Asean and China have formal cultural cooperation arrangements and have highlighted people-to-people exchanges. Such programs should create reciprocal opportunities: joint research, scholarships across disciplines, artist residencies, school partnerships, heritage preservation and regional reporting fellowships. Participants should come from rural communities and minority groups as well as capitals and elite universities. Honest cultural exchange can build trust, while independent media literacy and open discussion help societies resist stereotypes and disinformation without surrendering scrutiny of state conduct. Social diplomacy matters because people experience geopolitics through livelihoods and safety. Governments can cooperate on migrant worker protection, trafficking, online scam networks, public health, food security, disaster preparedness and education. These problems hit vulnerable people first. Asean and China should create practical channels among labor ministries, police, health agencies and civil society, with safeguards for rights and due process. Smaller groups can pilot hotlines, worker information services or disaster drills in border regions, then bring the lessons to Asean for common standards. Success should be judged by safer workers, faster assistance and more secure communities. A shared regional agenda can also prevent protection from depending on any government’s bilateral favor. Environmental diplomacy is equally urgent. Forest fires and haze, river flows, marine plastics, biodiversity loss, extreme heat and stronger storms ignore national boundaries. The Asean-China environmental strategy for 2026–2030 identifies cooperation in green technology, circular economy, finance and alignment of trade with climate commitments. Asean should insist on open environmental data, independent monitoring, community consultation and measurable targets across projects, including those negotiated bilaterally. Mekong countries can pursue basin-level cooperation on timely hydrological data and ecological impacts, while coastal states and China can expand scientific work on shared marine ecosystems. Every project should disclose who benefits, who bears costs and how affected communities can seek remedy. Multilateral diplomacy must set the region’s floor: international law, peaceful settlement, inclusive institutions and standards no member will quietly trade away. Minilateral cooperation can help directly affected states move sooner, provided their work returns to Asean and raises its capacity to act. Bilateral engagement remains necessary for specific disputes and agreements. But if each government treats a concession as its private gain or a maritime incident as another state’s private problem, China can deal with them one by one. Asean needs consultations before negotiations, information on proposed agreements and a habit of responding when any member faces pressure. Common principles acquire force only when members defend them together. The test is not whether Asean can erase its differences with China. It cannot. The test is whether those differences will let a much larger power choose the terms of engagement separately with each member. Asean will negotiate collectively, coordinate selectively, speak candidly and cooperate where interests converge. It can pair credible defense and legal positions with open economic exchange, social protection, ecological stewardship and genuine cultural contact. Diplomacy across all tracks gives Southeast Asia more ways to shape outcomes, but its center must hold. If Asean will not stand behind its own common positions, members become easier to isolate. Unity must be practiced before the next crisis, not merely invoked during one. The author is a professor at UP Los Baños and vice chairman of the board of PTVNI.

results.title: House honors Tacloban school shooting victim
results.description: THE House of Representatives adopted a resolution honoring 15-year-old Scout Chris Lorenz Tanglao Fabian, who was killed while trying to protect his classmates during the June 22 shooting at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City. House Resolution 1464, consolidated with HR 1176, and adopted on Tuesday (Sept. 29), recognized Fabian’s actions during the attack when he rushed to secure his classroom door as armed assailants approached, helping keep his classmates inside safe. The June 22 shooting left three students dead and several others injured. HR 1464 was filed by Speaker Faustino Dy III, Majority Leader Ferdinand Alexander Marcos and Minority Leader Marcelino Libanan, while HR 1176 was filed by Leyte 1st District Rep. Ferdinand Martin Romualdez and Tingog Party-list Reps. Yedda Marie Romualdez, Andrew Julian Romualdez and Jude Acidre. Acidre said the House recognition honored Fabian’s concern for his classmates despite the danger he faced. “In the midst of a dangerous situation, Chris thought of his classmates’ safety. He was young, but his courage and love for others were great,” Acidre said. The Boy Scouts of the Philippines had earlier posthumously given Fabian the Gold Gallantry and Heroism Award, while the Tacloban City government declared him a “Young Hero” in August.

results.title: Conrad Manila introduces Orkidéa, its signature craft gin
results.description: AS part of the hotel’s 10th anniversary celebrations, Conrad Manila proudly introduces Orkidéa, its signature craft gin exclusively available at C Lounge starting Sept. 25, 2026. Inspired by the Philippine orchid, this bespoke spirit is crafted with indigenous botanicals, reflecting the richness of local craftsmanship and the diverse flavors of the Philippine archipelago. “Marking our 10th anniversary gave us an opportunity to create something that is distinctly Conrad Manila and deeply connected to the Philippines,” said Rupert Hallam, general manager of Conrad Manila. “Orkidéa brings together local ingredients, craftsmanship, and creativity in a way that feels both celebratory and personal. Whether guests discover it in a cocktail at C Lounge or take a bottle home, we wanted it to reflect the richness of Philippine botanicals and the artistry behind local craft distilling.” Distilled in partnership with Full Circle Craft Distillers Co. Inc. in Calamba, Laguna, Orkidéa is crafted using locally sourced ingredients, including calamansi from Pangasinan, pandan from Laguna, sampaguita from Antipolo, and other carefully selected botanicals. Delicate floral notes are balanced by layers of lemongrass from Cavite and Benguet pine from Sagada, resulting in a refined and contemporary spirit that captures the vibrant character of the Philippines. Created as a tribute to Conrad Manila’s decade of exceptional guest experiences, Orkidéa reflects the property’s enduring pursuit of excellence, attention to detail and deep appreciation for local culture.

results.title: 3,500 jins set to clash at Milo National meet
results.description: THE drive to develop the next generation of taekwondo champions continues as the Philippine Taekwondo Association (PTA) stages the 2026 Milo National Taekwondo Championships this October. The two-part national tournament is expected to draw around 3,500 young athletes from all affiliated chapters and branches across the country, including representatives from 20 regions and the National Capital Region. The Kyorugi (Free Sparring) competition will be held on Oct. 3 and 4 at the Ninoy Aquino Stadium, while the Poomsae (Forms) competition is set for Oct. 11 at the Ninoy Aquino Stadium. Milo and the Philippine Taekwondo Association, under the leadership of Grandmaster Hong, have joined forces in supporting the development of Filipino youth. Through this partnership, the event has provided valuable support to its grassroots program, helping create opportunities for young athletes to develop their skills, discipline and passion for taekwondo. Grandmaster Hong, who has been at the forefront of PTA’s programs the past five decades, is excited to see taekwondo jins from different parts of the country vie for honors in their respective divisions. Kyorugi will feature Toddler, Grade School, Cadet and Junior categories for both boys and girls, with each age group divided into Novice and Advanced divisions. The Poomsae competition, meanwhile, will showcase Recognized Poomsae and Freestyle Poomsae in the Toddler, Grade School, Cadet and Junior age groups. Competition begins at 9 a.m. on both events, with the official opening ceremony scheduled for 1 p.m. on Oct. 3 and highlighted by a special performance from the Philippine Demonstration Team.

results.title: When bank secrecy yields to justice
results.description: Dear PAO, I am writing to seek your advice regarding my daughter, who became a victim of alleged human trafficking committed by a foreign national here in the Philippines. In the course of the proceedings, we learned that the foreigner maintained a foreign currency deposit with a Philippine bank, which may contain transactions relevant to the case and which could potentially be used to satisfy the damages that may be awarded to my daughter. However, when the issue of examining or obtaining his bank records was raised, the foreigner claimed that his accounts were confidential; hence, could not be examined or garnished. Is his claim correct? Mae Dear Mae, Section 8 of Republic Act (RA) 6426, or the Foreign Currency Deposit Act of the Philippines, provides, as a general rule, that foreign currency deposits are absolutely confidential in nature and cannot be examined, inquired into, or looked into by any person except upon the written permission of the depositor. In addition, foreign currency deposits are also exempt from attachment, garnishment, or any other order or process of any court, legislative body, government agency, or administrative body. Aside from the foregoing, it is also important to make reference to the pronouncement of the Supreme Court in Salvacion v. Central Bank of the Philippines, China Banking Corporations and Greg Bartelli, GR 94723, Aug. 21, 1997, written by Associate Justice Justo Torres Jr., where it was expounded that the application of the law depends on the extent of its justice. The garnishment of foreign currency deposits shall be allowed in extraordinary cases in order to prevent injustice; otherwise, it would negate Article 10 of the New Civil Code, which provides that “in case of doubt in the interpretation or application of laws, it is presumed that the lawmaking body intended right and justice to prevail.” Moreover, RA 9208, as amended by RA 11862, otherwise known as the “Expanded Anti-Trafficking in Persons Act of 2022,” limited the strict confidential nature of foreign currency deposits vis-à-vis investigation of human trafficking cases. Section 9 (d) thereof states in part: “Notwithstanding the provisions of Republic Act No. 1405 as amended, Republic Act No. 6426 as amended, Republic Act No. 8791 and other pertinent laws, the LEAs investigating cases of trafficking in persons may inquire into or examine any particular deposit or investment, including related accounts, with any banking institution or non-bank financial institution; or require financial intermediaries, internet payment system providers, and other financial facilitators to provide financial documents and information, upon order of any competent court based on an ex parte application in cases of violations of this Act, when it has been established that there is reasonable ground to believe that the deposit or investments, including related accounts involved, are related to trafficking in persons and violations of this Act.” (Emphasis supplied) The Foreign Currency Deposit Act was enacted to encourage legitimate foreign currency deposits and investments; it was not intended to provide a means for a wrongdoer to evade one’s lawful obligations or defeat a victim’s lawful claim for damages. Accordingly, the foreign currency deposit may, in appropriate circumstances, be examined and garnished pursuant to proper judicial process, particularly where its continued protection would result in grave injustice and would effectively prevent the victim from enforcing a valid judgment for damages. A person should not be permitted to use the Foreign Currency Deposit Act as a shield to evade civil liability arising from his or her own wrongful conduct. In the present case, therefore, the foreign currency deposits of the suspect may be examined if there is reasonable ground to believe that the same were used for or in connection with human trafficking activities. Later on, the deposits may also be garnished if warranted by extraordinary circumstances in order to prevent injustice. The protection granted by the law should not be construed as extending to the point of allowing a wrongdoer to use it to escape criminal and civil liability. We hope that we were able to answer your queries. This advice was solely based on the facts you have narrated and our appreciation of the same. Our opinion may vary when other facts are changed or elaborated. Thank you for your continued trust and support. Editor’s note: Dear PAO is a daily column of the Public Attorney’s Office. Questions for Chief Acosta may be sent to dearpao@manilatimes.net

results.title: Obiena grateful after Asiad defense
results.description: UNDER wet conditions due to a drizzly Tuesday evening, Ernest John “EJ” Obiena still claimed his second straight men’s pole vault title in the 20th Asian Games in Japan. The Filipino pole vault ace did it in a record-setting fashion at the Nagoya City Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium. Obiena secured the gold medal after Chinese Yao Jie and Li Chenyang struck out at 5.75 m which the Philippine bet cleared in just one try. The 30-year-old decided to post a new meet record and successfully did so with a 5.91-meter (m) clearance, surpassing the 5.90-m height he aced in the previous edition in Hangzhou, China, back in 2023. Obiena thus gave the Philippines its third overall gold in the ongoing meet following gymnast Carlos Yulo’s floor exercise and vault titles. “A gold and a GR (games record) here in Nagoya,” wrote Obiena in his social media pages on Wednesday morning. “As athletes, we live in these moments. Moments that make us overthink, stress us, adrenaline pumping pressure on our backs and sometimes ... just sometimes pure joy. I take these moments as a blessing. This is what keeps me going back for more.” Obiena expressed gratitude to his team as well as the Filipinos for supporting him. “To all of the 110 million Filipinos, maraming salamat po (thank you so much) for making these moments possible. Competing is one thing, but competing for something greater, for the Philippines, is a privilege that I do not take lightly. For the country.” Obiena surpassed the 5.90-m height thrice this season, which he ended with this Asiad gold. Bouncing back from a lackluster 2025, the 6-foot-2 pole vaulter from Tondo collected 10 golds this year as he continued his resurgence. “What I felt today, it’s been a while, and to be honest I missed it,” Obiena said to POC Media. “With that, I think it’s bit of a reborn that I see the sport in a much different perspective than it was, a little bit of fun and reality”
